paperTitle: Singapore-Cambridge GCE O-Level 1184 English Language — AI-authored Practice Paper 35: The Provision Shop (Paper 2 §B style)

sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [15 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
Ah Seng's provision shop sat at the foot of our block in Bedok, wedged between the coffee shop and the lift landing, its doorway so narrow that two people could not pass through at once. Inside, the air was thick with the smell of dried mushrooms, brown soap and the sweet dust of biscuits sold loose from the tin. I had been sent there for small errands since I was tall enough to hold a coin — a packet of salt, a bulb for the kitchen, ten cents' worth of sweets kept in a fat glass jar by the till.

Paragraph 2
Ah Seng himself seemed as old as the shop. He knew every family on our street by name and by habit: whose mother liked which brand of oyster sauce, whose father had not yet paid for last week's cigarettes. That last kind he recorded in a thick exercise book, its columns filled with names and figures in his careful hand, for he would let a neighbour take what they needed and settle it when the salary came at the end of the month. Whenever I paid, he would drop an extra sweet into my palm without a word, as though it were a secret between us.

Paragraph 3
As the years passed, the street changed around him. A gleaming supermarket opened two bus stops away, its aisles wide and its trolleys deep, and my mother began to buy our rice and oil there by the trolley-load. Later still, boxes of groceries started arriving at our door, ordered from a phone and carried up by a delivery man. Ah Seng's customers dwindled. The shop that had once buzzed each evening grew quiet, and the fat glass jar by the till was often full to the brim.

Paragraph 4
I was walking home from school when I saw the notice, a square of cardboard taped inside the glass in Ah Seng's careful hand. The shop would close at the end of the month. I stood on the pavement longer than I meant to, reading those few short words again and again, as though staring might change them.

Paragraph 5
On the last Saturday I went in. The shelves stood half-bare, like a mouth with missing teeth, and cardboard cartons were stacked where the sacks of rice used to lean. Ah Seng was wrapping a set of enamel bowls in old newspaper, his movements slow and unhurried, as if he had all the time in the world and none of it left.

Paragraph 6
'Come,' he said, and reached beneath the counter. He brought out the thick exercise book, its pages now yellowed and soft at the corners, and turned to an early page. There, in a child's wobbling pencil beside a row of his neat figures, was my own name — I had once insisted on signing for a packet of sweets myself, copying the grown-ups, years before I could properly write. He had kept the book all this time. I did not know what to say, so I said nothing, and he only smiled and closed it gently.

Paragraph 7
Walking home, I understood at last what the little shop had been. It was never only a place to buy salt and light bulbs. It was a place where an old man had watched me grow from a coin-clutching child into someone taller than his counter, and had marked the whole of it down, quietly, in an exercise book no supermarket would ever keep.

Paragraph 8
At the end of the month the metal shutter came down for the last time, a final full stop under a long sentence. A bubble-tea shop stands there now, bright and busy, and the young people queuing outside have never heard of Ah Seng. But when I pass, I still catch, or imagine I catch, the faint smell of dried mushrooms and brown soap — and for a moment I am small again, holding out a warm coin to a man who always had a sweet to spare.

(Glossary: provision shop: a small neighbourhood grocery, once common at the foot of Singapore HDB blocks, selling everyday goods and often letting regular customers buy on credit.)

questions.stem: Q1. From Paragraph 1, where was Ah Seng's provision shop located? [1]
questions.answer: at the foot of the narrator's block in Bedok, between the coffee shop and the lift landing (any one location detail earns the mark)

questions.stem: Q2. From Paragraph 4, when was the shop going to close? [1]
questions.answer: at the end of the month

questions.stem: Q3. What does the word 'dwindled' in 'Ah Seng's customers dwindled' (Paragraph 3) suggest about the number of customers? [1]
questions.answer: it steadily grew fewer and fewer / gradually decreased

questions.stem: Q4. What does the word 'wedged' in 'wedged between the coffee shop and the lift landing' (Paragraph 1) suggest about the shop? [1]
questions.answer: it was tightly squeezed / fitted into a very narrow space between the two

questions.stem: Q5. What does the word 'yellowed' tell us about the exercise book Ah Seng brought out in Paragraph 6? [1]
questions.answer: that it was very old / had aged over many years

questions.stem: Q6. Using your own words, explain why Ah Seng was willing to let neighbours take goods without paying at once. (Paragraph 2) [2]
questions.answer: MP1 (goodwill/trust): he trusted his neighbours and, out of kindness, let them have what they needed even when they could not pay straight away; MP2 (practical timing): he knew they were paid only once a month, so he let them settle the bill when their salary came in — accommodating that they were temporarily short of cash. Award one mark per distinct point.

questions.stem: Q7. Using your own words, explain why Ah Seng's shop 'grew quiet' over the years. (Paragraph 3) [2]
questions.answer: MP1: a large modern supermarket opened nearby and drew his customers away; MP2: later, people could order groceries by phone and have them delivered to their door, so they no longer needed his small shop. Award one mark per distinct competitor/reason; 'more convenient' is acceptable within MP2.

questions.stem: Q8. Using your own words, explain what the narrator realised the shop had truly meant to him, as described in Paragraph 7. [2]
questions.answer: MP1: it was far more than a place to buy goods — it was somewhere he was recognised and treated as an individual, not just a customer; MP2: an old man had watched him grow up over the years and quietly kept a record of him, giving him a sense of belonging that a supermarket could never provide. Award one mark per distinct point.

questions.stem: Q9. What is the effect of describing the half-empty shelves as 'like a mouth with missing teeth' (Paragraph 5)? [2]
questions.answer: the simile creates a vivid, slightly sad image of gaps and incompleteness, making the emptying shop seem damaged and diminished, and hinting at loss and decay

questions.stem: Q10. What is the effect of calling the closing shutter 'a final full stop under a long sentence' (Paragraph 8)? [2]
questions.answer: the metaphor compares the shop's decades of life to a long sentence, so the shutter closing becomes its definite ending — emphasising finality and that a long chapter of the neighbourhood's history is now firmly over

sections.instruction: Q11. [4 marks in total] The narrator's dominant feeling changes as the passage moves from his childhood memories of the shop to its final closing. For each moment below, go back to the relevant paragraphs of the narrative and choose ONE word from the bank that best describes his dominant feeling there. Some words in the bank are not used, and each word may be used once only. Word bank: amused / annoyed / dismayed / fond / indifferent / proud / touched / wistful.
sections.passage: Refer to the same 'The Provision Shop' narrative in Exercise 1 above. Read the paragraphs named in each question, then choose the single word from the bank that best describes how the narrator feels at that moment.
